  "title": "MPs deny Commons vote means animals are not recognised as sentient",
  "summary": "A Commons vote on the European Union (Withdrawal) Bill has sparked confusion and protest after an amendment to carry over the EU's animal sentience protocol into UK law was defeated. Ministers and MPs insist the outcome was procedural and does not change the government's recognition of animal sentience.",
  "body": "MPs have been forced to deny that a Commons vote last week means animals are not recognised in the UK as sentient life forms. An amendment to the European Union (Withdrawal) Bill to transfer the EU protocol on animal sentience into UK law was defeated by 313 votes to 295 on 15 November, and since then a row has developed as to what the vote meant in practice.

Several Conservative figures moved quickly to counter coverage they described as misleading. Zac Goldsmith called some of the reporting “weird and dishonest” and tweeted that the vote concerned the correct legal procedure for ensuring animal welfare standards – not the principle of whether animals are sentient. Rachel Maclean, MP for Redditch, posted a video accusing critics of spreading “fake news” and said: “This government, and in fact all governments, are deeply committed to continuing to protect animals as sentient beings. That law is already written into our own law.”

Prime Minister Theresa May reiterated that position at Wednesday’s prime minister’s questions, saying: “We recognise and respect that animals are sentient beings, and should be treated accordingly.” Tory MP Hugo Swire also shared a letter he said he had received from the environment secretary, Michael Gove, and added: “I do not believe that any MP thinks that animals do not have feelings or emotions.”

Despite these reassurances, the Commons defeat has prompted protests from animal rights groups and the public. Multiple online petitions aimed at the House of Lords, parliament and the environment secretary attracted signatures, and public figures including presenter Sue Perkins voiced strong criticism of MPs over the issue.

The British Veterinary Association expressed alarm at the outcome. Gudrun Ravetz, the association’s senior vice-president, said: “It is extremely concerning that a marginal majority of MPs have voted-down this seminal clause. This action undermines the government’s previous promises that the UK will continue to be known for our high standards of animal health and welfare post-Brexit.”

Supporters of the government’s position argued that incorporating the EU text verbatim was not the only route to maintaining high welfare standards. Henry Smith, the Conservative MP for Crawley, pointed out that EU law still permitted practices across Europe that animal rights groups oppose, implying that the amendment was not a straightforward improvement.

The defeated amendment was tabled by a group of MPs including Green party co-leader Caroline Lucas. It sought specifically to incorporate article 13 of title II of the Lisbon treaty into UK law. During debate on the amendment, Lucas highlighted the clause’s origins in the UK’s 1997 presidency of the EU and noted that since 1999 EU law had explicitly recognised animals as sentient beings.

With Brexit negotiations and the wider process of converting EU-derived law to domestic statute still under way, the episode has exposed political fault lines over how best to secure animal welfare after the UK leaves the EU. Ministers insist there is no change in policy on recognising animal sentience; animal welfare campaigners say the Commons vote has nevertheless weakened public confidence and are urging peers in the House of Lords to press for stronger, explicit protections.",
  "last_updated": "2018-11-16"
}
